messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Harris first met Eleanor in her late autumn, a woman whose life had been built on precision and control. At seventy-six, she was a retired radiologist, a profession that had rewarded her meticulous eye and her ability to see danger hidden in plain sight—a shadow on a lung, a fracture line barely visible. But the danger she now scanned for was not on an X-ray. It was everywhere else. The trauma that had rewired her world had happened three years prior, during a brief visit to a city that erupted into armed conflict while she was there. She had been caught in a crossfire in a marketplace, pinned behind a concrete planter for what felt like hours, the air thick with smoke and the sound of automatic weapons. A man next to her, a stranger, had been shot in the head. She remembered the wet, percussive sound of the bullet striking bone, the way his body slumped, the blood spreading across the white stone. What she could not do, however, was retrieve the memory in any orderly way. When she tried to deliberately recall that day, her mind went blank, a white wall of static. The memory existed only as a series of fragments—the smell of cordite, the sensation of grit against her cheek, the unbearable heat of the sun on her neck—but it would not come together as a story. She could not put it into words. The shame that accompanied these involuntary flashes was profound; she felt a deep, irrational sense of culpability, as if her very survival had been a form of cowardice.

Because she could not control the memory, Eleanor had come to believe that the only way to manage it was to control everything else. Her avoidance had become a full-time occupation. She had stopped making any plans for the future, refusing to book a vacation or even a dinner reservation more than a day in advance, because the act of looking ahead felt like an invitation for catastrophe. She spent long hours on her tablet, playing solitaire or scrolling through news feeds, a screen that served as a barrier between her and the intrusive fragments. When the memory surfaced—a sudden, unbidden image of the man’s face—she would immediately reach for her phone, the act of swiping and tapping a ritual that allowed her to escape the feeling. This, in turn, deepened the problem. By refusing to engage with the memory, she never practiced the act of recalling it on her own terms, which made the involuntary intrusions feel even more alien and terrifying when they broke through. The shame grew, too, because she felt she was hiding from something she should have been able to face.

The memory also dictated her sense of threat. The world outside her home had become a field of potential ambushes. She constantly scanned her surroundings for signs of danger, her eyes darting from person to person, from doorway to doorway, a clinical vigilance that exhausted her. She avoided unfamiliar places entirely, because she could not pre-assess the risk. Even a simple trip to a new grocery store felt like navigating a minefield. She felt threatened by strangers approaching her, even in ordinary situations; a person asking for directions on the street would make her heart pound and her breath catch. This hypervigilance, in turn, fed back into her memory. The more she scanned for danger, the more her brain was primed to interpret any ambiguous cue—a raised voice, a sudden movement—as a signal of returning threat, which would trigger a flash of the marketplace, the sound of the gunshot, the feeling of the concrete against her back. Her threat-monitoring was not a neutral state; it was a mechanism that repeatedly activated the traumatic memory, keeping the wound fresh.

The cycle had become self-reinforcing. Her avoidance of feelings and plans meant she had no buffer against the threat, and her constant scanning meant she was never truly safe. The only way Eleanor had found to quiet the loop was to retreat further into her strategies. She told Dr. Harris that she had not left her house in over two weeks, except to sit in her backyard, where she could see all approaches. She had stopped answering the phone. Her husband, a kind but bewildered man, had taken over all the shopping and errands, but he could not understand why she would not even talk about what had happened. What finally brought Eleanor to seek help was not the fear, but the shame. She had realized, with a clarity that felt like another blow, that she was disappearing. The woman who had once diagnosed cancer from a shadow was now afraid of a stranger’s glance. She was not living; she was hiding. What she feared most was that there was no way out of the loop—that the memory would always be in control. What she hoped for, barely daring to admit it, was that Dr. Harris might help her find a way to look at it, just once, without being destroyed.
